iem-juzear-61t.review: Very balanced. Not as blunt as the Tea 2. The bass punch is right in quantity and quality: not a lot, but just right, with more rumble than the 41T or Tea 2, though not as much as the Tea Pro. Good imaging; the soundstage is right there with the Tea 2 and cheaper. Cleaner mids. Very natural sound. The timbre is OK, not as plasticky and blunt as the Tea 2. More fun and less neutral than the Tea 2 or 41T, but not basshead either; just right. Weaknesses: the fit is actually fine, it just needs the right eartips; and I wish the separation had more contrast. But at this budget it's crazy good. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-ziigaat-odyssey-2.review: Good. JM-1 target. Better timbre and fit than the Daybreak. Technicalities slightly better than the Daybreak, but the price is waaay higher, bruv. (Full review on his YouTube.)

iem-juzear-light-shuttle.review: Coherent. Somewhat JM-1 in the mids, but I find it a little muddy: low-mids to sub-bass are a bit high, the lower treble is a bit high too, and the air treble is fairly boosted. Not bad; I just prefer the Daybreak, which is a bit cleaner in overall tonality. The upper-treble timbre isn't that natural either.

iem-epz-p50.review: Rich highs, great clarity and resolution. Wider and more spacious than the 61T. The bass impact isn't lost; it's well extended but not the main highlight. Fast, detailed bass transients. Open, clear sound. Rock sounds crunchy, like switching on a light overdrive to make it aggressive, or like tape saturation in mastering. The highs are good, nothing like the Supermix 4, and it doesn't feel thin. The main emphasis, mids to highs, is good. Mid-bass to sub isn't the star, but it's not bad either; it plays its part.

iem-epz-p40.review: Harman bright. The default tonality isn't to my liking: very bright. But the treble roll-off is good, not pointy mountain peaks and dips, just a straight sloping descent. And if you EQ it: verrrry good. It only takes 2 or 3 EQ bands: a high-shelf roll-off to cut the treble and a small mid lift. Check my squig.link page. Done.

iem-erand-resonance-5.review: U-shaped: a tuning that emphasises the very bottom of the sub-bass and the top of the treble, with a recessed midrange. So it feels like lots of sub and top-end treble. Highly coherent. The high-frequency timbre is still planar, which doesn't sit well with my ears. Compared with the P40 when both are EQ'd, the P40's timbre is better, more accurate and slightly wider; separation on the Erand is a bit blurry. Not a bad IEM though. The treble roll-off is good, so a high-shelf cut plus a midrange lift is enough.

iem-xenns-mangird-tea-2.review: One of the highly regarded, underrated IEMs in the audiophile world. Wide, grand, deep. Better instrument separation, timbre and treble detail. Deep sub-bass, good punch. Extraordinary, holographic technicalities: when guitar and keyboard play together you can clearly tell which is which. Male vocals become clearer. Better, thick lower mids. Better bass and soundstage than the Blessing 3 too (personal preference).

iem-epz-530.review: SUPERB IEM FIT, and versatile with its cable: swappable 3.5 / 2.5 / 4.4 mm plugs, very practical. Smooth sound in the upper mids; the treble is sparkly but smooth, not aggressive, not piercing. Good timbre too for an all-5-BA set. Good punch, fast sub-bass, though a shame it doesn't go quite deep enough without a DD. But the fit is too good to skip, and the sound is very friendly for monitoring!

iem-64-audio-u12t.review: I'm gonna say this is the best traditional IEM ever made (or that I've ever tried). That spacious, free, very OPEN character up top: nobody else can make it except 64 Audio. Very distinctive. All balanced-armature drivers, yet the bass is plenty and already very OK. Balanced, fast, clear, not painful. The fit isn't as big as the U18s or U18t, which is why it's here. LID technology keeps it sounding its best on any source, and APEX lets you swap modules for how much outside sound gets in, which also raises or lowers the bass.

iem-sennheiser-ie600.review: The best single DD I have ever tried. The vocals don't stand apart and forward like most Chinese brands. Champion technicalities. Fast bass. Very well balanced, and coherent of course, since no other driver needs a crossover. Driver resolution: Sennheiser's research on transducers and back volume. Top German quality control (confirmed by talking to Sennheiser's Southeast Asia leadership when I attended the MTW3 launch in August 2022).

iem-moondrop-blessing-3.review: Still fairly close in tuning to the Blessing 2: leaning neutral with a bass boost. But the bass is DEEP and fast; you FEEL it even if there isn't a lot. Clean upper mids, better than the Tea 2. Clarity is OK. Weaknesses for me: the lower mids aren't as thick as the Tea 2 (personal preference), and some people may still find the bass too little. But it's highly coherent, a good crossover, no sense of missing frequencies. Lovely soundstage, though the Tea 2 is still slightly better. If you like some bass, get the Tea 2; if you want bright, clean upper mids leaning neutral and are vocals-only, get this. Same class; it's down to preference.

iem-simgot-supermix-5.review: The lower-to-upper treble roll-off is good. Mid-bass to sub-bass is clean, in the direction of the Tea Pro SE, Mega7 etc. But the upper mids mound up too high (check my squig.link), and I think the air treble could be boosted more. Main weakness: the upper mids at 3–4 kHz are still high. The fit is a bit big, and the bone conduction still hums a bit when touched.

iem-ziigaat-odyssey.review: Coherency is 80%, fine. Big, fat bass. I think the 61T's BA-to-DD crossover transition is still tidier; this has waaay more highs than the 61T. Good. Can be used for monitoring; better fit than the 61T. The 61T's timbre is more natural, and you hear the mid-bass and mids more there; this one has much more, fatter bass and more sparkle up top. Better fit and better technicalities than the 61T. Above this sits the EPZ P50, spacious and satisfying. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-kiwi-ears-quintet.review: Fairly coherent, not patchy, no sense of something missing. Thick, deep sub-bass but not basshead. Clear treble, a nice sparkle. If you want a cool sub-bass extension with very clear treble, go for it: the PZT and planar in the treble are very good. Clear, but careful: at loud volume it can be fatiguing. Weakness for me: the mid-bass lacks punch and the low-mids aren't as crunchy and thick as the Tea 2; the energy is only in the sub-bass and treble, the mids lack meat. Very good timbre.

iem-juzear-41t.review: FINALLY, A MINI TEA 2! Warm-balanced, tuned very much like the Tea 2. Where the SR5 has some sharpness at 8 kHz and lacks lower mids, this has none of that. The 4BA + 1DD tuning that suits me best, and very nice for monitoring too: accurate, good imaging and soundstage, though not as aggressive, crunchy, wide and spacious as the Tea 2. Is it better than the SR5? For me, yes. Some might miss the 8 kHz treble brightness. The fit is AMAZING for monitoring; no need to swap cables or tips. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-pula-pa02.review: Good. Neutral, natural midrange, with more vocal emphasis and a fairly boosted treble sizzle, though not as boosted as the Supermix 4. The transition from upper mids/treble down to the lows is lacking a little: not quite full-sounding. Coherency is actually OK but could be better; people who can't hear coherency much may not notice. It's good: natural, a lovely faceplate, and the fit works well on stage.

iem-sound-rhyme-sr5.review: A 4-way crossover, HIGHLY COHERENT: not messy, no patchiness or missing frequencies. For 2 million rupiah, 5 drivers this coherent. Bright at 8 kHz: a tad of boost there, not piercing but dominant. Smooth top-end treble on cymbals, clear, not aggressive. Good midrange; guitars sound aggressive. KNOWLES BA, BABY! The sub-bass boost isn't big but the DD quality is superb: deep and thick. Sub-bass-centric (under 80 Hz), not much mid-bass around 100–150 Hz. Lovely vocals, and the bass comes through. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-gizaudio-chopin.review: Lovers of very forward vocals plus lots of sub-bass, while still balanced and not basshead, can take this. Very Gizaudio tuning: deep, plentiful sub-bass, but it can't be called basshead yet. The nicest thing is the fit: its shape hangs in the ear rather than hugging it like the SR5.

iem-tangzu-heyday.review: Now this is the best planar I've tried so far. No need for the Timeless any more, or the Raptgo, TRN Kirin or Tin P1. Just this. Pleasant, bright and clear, lovely, and the soundstage technicalities are extraordinarily good: holographic, fast, crunchy. Great for vocals, all genres, fast bass. For rock with distortion, fuzz and overdrive it's insanely good. The space: the reverb and soundstage are really grand. With AET08 tips the treble comes down to just right: not painful, but not lacking either.

iem-crinear-nightfall.tagline: Best fun JM-1 at 1 million rupiah
iem-crinear-nightfall.review: A candidate for best at 1 million. A clean, tidy all-rounder with somewhat thick sub-bass. A veeery safe tuning. Warm treble; the sub feels a bit thick because there isn't much treble. Technicalities are fairly wide, competing with the C7. The fit is far nicer than the C7 and T6. Better eartips for me: Infitear IE45 Pro. For stage depth forward and up, the T6 is still slightly better, but the T6's upper mids can be too shouty; the Nightfall is safer for me. A very, very all-rounder. (Full review on his YouTube.)

iem-tin-hifi-c7.review: Basically the same as the Tin T6 with the pink nozzle; the tuning isn't far off. The T6's soundstage is a tiiiny bit better, with more dimension forward and upward. This one's fit is better: full resin, no metal like the T6. You can't swap nozzle filters, and the cable is 2-pin, not QDC. The timbre is more natural and smooth, less metallic in the highs, even when both are EQ'd to the same target. Your choice; both are good.

iem-tinhifi-t6.review: Hiiighly coherent: the planar and dynamic drivers feel completely unified. Very wide, open sound in the midrange. Lots of upper mids and sub-bass, not much low-mids. Similar to the Tangzu Red Lion WITHOUT the excessive air boost. Cleaner mid-bass, and safer air treble than the EW300. If you like the sub and mid-bass lower and closer to the upper mids, the Xuan NV is still very good too.

iem-truthear-nova.tagline: Used by Barasuara and Vega Antares (Dewa)
iem-truthear-nova.review: Versus the SR5 this is more open up top, in the upper-mid staging and vocals, with much deeper sub-bass. The vocals sit further back than the SR5, which is more forward. If you find the SR5's bass lacking punch, take this. Fairly fun-sounding. Very nice if you like a relaxed volume; if you love it really loud it can get a bit shouty/sibilant in the upper mids. Thick for listening to guitars. Used by Iga Massardi, Gerald Situmorang, Vega Antares, TJ Kusuma and Ichyl Asteriska. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-tangzu-xuan-nv.review: NATURAL TIMBRE DYNAMICS! Clear separation, natural timbre, grand and luxurious. A bit hard to drive. Better than the DZ4 and C3, and I find its natural treble timbre nicer than the Sonus. The Sonus is in the same class, but I prefer this one's imaging. BA treble vs DD treble is personal taste, but the Sonus has a bit less mid-bass. This is thicker but not muddy, and safer from shoutiness than the Sonus (and even then you have to push the Sonus very loud before it's shouty). Its weakness: a bit hard to drive. (Review on his YouTube.)

iem-soratune-yi01.review: This, the EW300 and the Xuan NV are the same class. The best bass if you want fun: rumble, bass timbre, good bass technicalities, plus really lovely treble breadth and openness. Volume linearity: it doesn't need to be as loud as the Xuan NV. If you like it loud, the Xuan's treble is safer. The fit is far better than the Xuan and EW300. Two followers DM'd me saying it easily develops channel imbalance (you've been warned); I've only tried it in a shop. Fun and technically very good. The DD timbre is slightly less flat than the Xuan: more sparkle and more bottom end than the Xuan, but the treble sizzle isn't as metallic as the EW300. Skip the BL02: too V-shaped with metallic timbre.

iem-simgot-ew300.review: Similar to the Xuan NV: airier treble with less natural treble timbre, but a more open-sounding soundstage. The mid-bass gets a bit crumpled; not very muffled, just more than the Xuan NV, whose mid-bass is cleaner. Imaging about the same. Easier to drive than the Xuan NV. For bass and mid-bass I prefer the Xuan NV; for upper mids to treble technicality and soundstage, this one's better; for treble timbre naturalness, the Xuan NV. Choose your poison. (Review on his YouTube. The black HBB version sounds the same.)

iem-moondrop-lan-2.review: Still very Moondrop: the upper mids rise early from 1 kHz. The VDSF target, with nasal mids and very high vocals in the midrange. Moondrop drivers are never bad; the tuning is just the same as usual. Not bad, there's a market for it. The Ref version is more neutral; the Pop version has more mid-bass to sub-bass.

iem-kinera-sol.review: The tonality is very close to the Kinera Wyvern Black/White, with a small low-mid bump due to the bone conduction inside the shell (it's a low-frequency driver; it doesn't vibrate like Shokz, it just adds sub-bass extension), but the bass quantity doesn't grow much. It won't be like the bone conduction in the 50-million Canpur. The mic is better: louder, 4 mic gain levels, and mic noise reduction too, though I think the Rays does it better. For the price it's OK for gamers and casual South-Jakarta-office-worker meetings. The colour isn't gamer-y either: black.

iem-simgot-eg280.tagline: Includes a DSP EQ dongle DAC
iem-simgot-eg280.review: This is actually OK. The tuning is similar to the EW300, with a lot of top-end treble that can be dangerous. But it comes with a dongle DAC with an 8-band parametric EQ, and a mic whose gain you can set in the app. Cool, Simgot: I thought the app couldn't rival FiiO/Moondrop, but it's really good. Shame the DAC's amp is small, like the Moondrop Echo; something like the Akliam PD6 might be wider, but then the price might not work. Mid-bass to sub-bass is also similar to the EW300 or LM500: the mids dip around 800 Hz and rise gradually from the low-mids to the sub.

iem-agasound-sublimation.review: A very upper-mid-to-lower-treble-centric type, so it's clear and forward in the vocals. If you're after very natural timbre, I think there's still a hint of metallic shrillness around 4–6 kHz. It's sort of the counter to the EW300, which has lots of sub and top treble but mids/upper mids that don't fill in much; the Sublimation instead bites with really bold upper mids to lower treble.

iem-etymotic.review: THE ONLY REAL NEUTRAL IEM. Only this one. Not the Dunu Titan S, not the HZSound Mirror. No. Only this. Its only weakness is the deep insertion; if you're not used to it, it's uncomfortable. But that's the technology that makes the treble roll-off right and neutral.

iem-raptgo-hook-x.review: This is also good. Compared with the Heyday I slightly prefer the Heyday; something here makes the upper midrange a bit muffled/warm. But if you can't stand the Heyday, maybe this one is for you.

iem-juzear-defiant.review: No problem with the tuning: a little in the direction of the 61T. But coherency is lacking: the low-mids go missing, with a lot of vocal emphasis. And the timbre is pretty bad, very plasticky, losing the definition you usually get from multi-BA IEMs at 3 million rupiah and up. The mids aren't tight, not well defined, not unified. The tuning's OK. If you only need the looks and the tuning, go ahead. My choice is still the trio: Xuan, EW300, Soratune.

iem-inawaken-mistwood.review: Same as the Inawaken Dawn MS; just a different faceplate, as far as I can tell. Feel free to take this or not, or step down to the Dawn MS. Very similar.

iem-pula-unicrom.review: Good driver. Tuned like the Inawaken Dawn MS, the type where the mid-bass rises early, but the bass recovers from its impact a bit slowly, so it seems to have a lot of mid-bass to sub. If you want clean mid-bass, this isn't a good fit; go to the Xuan NV or Soratune. Not as airy as the EW300 either. Average soundstage and imaging, but decent for the price.

iem-simgot-em6l.review: Not as bright as the EA500. Wide. Warm + balanced, which is definitely what I like. Crank the volume, it's fine. The 3D width, depth and positioning are good too. Coherency is fine; the timbre is still a bit plasticky. Really handsome. Downside? For lovers of neutral-bright sound it may be too warm.

iem-moondrop-kadenz.review: Moondrop VDSF; as usual I still don't like it. Still too midrange-y, not much sub. Very, very Moondrop. For a single DD at 2 million rupiah I don't recommend it: a bit overpriced. The fit isn't great, and the cable is stiff and heavy. The DSP dongle is OK. But I have to admit the soundstage and imaging are spacious, and the mids are bright, clear and clean, though for my taste the bass needs more punch from mid-bass to sub-bass.

iem-tangzu-zetian-wu.review: The first single planar I could enjoy on first listen without a lot of excuses about flaws. The sub-bass is OK, a bit much, but fast because it's planar. Very enjoyable. Crunchy electric guitars, a wide, open stage. I think it needs a bit more power to sound its best. SUPERB CLARITY: very clear even on murky/warm recordings. More sub-bass than the Heyday version.

iem-shuoer-s12.review: Rock is great on this. Planar timbre really is different; you have to try at least one planar. Planars are different: fast transients, no distortion, clear, and guitar twang is great here. Only the S12's treble is a bit high. I don't like the S12 Pro: its treble is even sharper. Best to get the pink one if you can.

iem-moondrop-aria-2.review: A single DD with good technicalities and good mids. Compared with the Aria 1, I prefer the Aria 1's bass quantity, and the Aria 1 sparkles more at the top of the treble, which can sting a bit for me. The Aria 2 handles the upper mids to treble well, but sadly the sub-bass was reduced too, whereas the Aria 1's was just right and kept it fun. For people who don't like a lot of sub-bass and focus on thick vocals, the Aria 2 is fine.

iem-7hz-sonus.review: Very transparent mids; a lovely, clean midrange, properly neutral with a sub-bass boost. The mid-bass is limp, not punchy, lacking weight. A spacious, open soundstage compared with the stock Dawn MS and C3. The weakness: not enough mid-bass for mid-bass lovers. But the upper mids to treble are truly spacious, open and bright. (IEM battle review on his YouTube.)

iem-tanchjim-4u.review: OK, actually. The treble suddenly drops off, maybe at 10 kHz, then suddenly gets pointy again around 12 kHz, so the treble is a bit crispy: singers' lip-smacking, like chewing, is very audible, and cymbals tizz too. Good, natural timbre. But for me the technicalities are just adequate, the bass lacks punch compared with the Xuan NV, and pushed loud it can get bright too. Not a bad sound though. If you like lots of treble, clean mids and not-very-punchy bass, this works.

iem-7hz-diablo.review: Ugh, no. Overdone mid-bass, very old-school. Not my tonal bias at all. Dirty in the low-mids, mid-bassy; I don't like it. And 6 kHz is dipped hard too. I think even the GK Kunten has a far better tuning than this.

iem-tin-hifi-dudu.review: I don't really like its treble roll-off; it's a bit untidy. But this is more balanced and cleaner, and low notes are heard more clearly than on the S08. Comes with a USB-C cable, of course; its DAC is ordinary and sounds a bit bright compared with switching to a 3.5 mm cable and a DAC like the Shanling UA1 Plus. Soundstage and imaging are still average; it didn't excite me like planars such as the 7Hz Timeless, Raptgo or Tangzu Heyday. But for the price it's OK to collect.
